story: A statewide poll found 73 percent of Alaska likely voters want new data center development paused, and nine days later the one Alaska council that voted on a data center ban rejected it 4 to 2 and passed a process objection instead

claims.claim: A Data for Progress survey found 73 percent of Alaska likely voters support pausing new data center development until the state passes a law regulating it.
claims.verbatim: Alaska voters support pausing new data center development until the state passes a law regulating it, with 73% in support, including 63% of Republicans.
claims.notes: Primary in that the pollster published its own survey. Deck says 'according to Data for Progress' because the exact question wording is not published anywhere reachable. See C09.

claims.claim: The same survey found 63 percent of Alaska Republicans support pausing new data center development until the state passes a law regulating it.
claims.verbatim: with 73% in support, including 63% of Republicans
claims.notes: Subgroup. No party level n or subgroup margin of error is published, so the true error on 63 percent is wider than the plus or minus 4 on the full sample.

claims.claim: The Data for Progress Alaska survey sampled 605 likely voters.
claims.verbatim: Data for Progress conducted a survey of 605 likely voters in Alaska using SMS and web panel respondents.
claims.notes: A simple random n of 605 yields a 95 percent margin of about plus or minus 3.98 points, which matches the stated plus or minus 4.

claims.claim: The Data for Progress Alaska survey was fielded from July 28th to August 4th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: From July 28 to August 4, 2026, Data for Progress conducted a survey of 605 likely voters in Alaska
claims.notes: Fielding closed nine days before the Houston vote and fourteen days before the primary, so the poll can't reflect either event.

claims.claim: The Data for Progress Alaska survey carries a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points.
claims.verbatim: The margin of error associated with the sample size is ±4 percentage points.
claims.notes: Applies to the full sample only, not to the party or borough subgroups used in C02 and C15 through C17.

claims.claim: The survey used SMS and web panel respondents and was weighted by age, gender, education, race, geography, and recalled vote.
claims.verbatim: The sample was weighted to be representative of likely voters by age, gender, education, race, geography, and recalled vote.
claims.notes: Opt in panel plus SMS, not probability sampling.

claims.claim: The Data for Progress Alaska survey was conducted in English only.
claims.verbatim: The survey was conducted in English.
claims.notes: A coverage limit in a state with substantial Alaska Native language speaking populations.

claims.claim: Data for Progress describes itself as equipping the progressive movement with the data and insights it needs to win.
claims.verbatim: Data for Progress equips the progressive movement with the data and insights it needs to win.
claims.notes: The organisation's own words on its own site. The single most important honesty line in the run.

claims.claim: Data for Progress did not publish the exact wording of the data center question in the post announcing the result.
claims.notes: Negative finding, so verbatim is null by nature. Phrase as 'the published post does not include the question wording' rather than 'the wording is secret'.

claims.claim: The share of Alaska voters worried about affording monthly utilities such as electricity or heat rose from 54 percent to 66 percent.
claims.verbatim: Worry about affording monthly utilities like electricity or heat has risen from 54% to 66%
claims.notes: Print as 'risen from 54 percent to 66 percent' without asserting the baseline month.

claims.claim: Worry about affording groceries and food rose from 61 percent to 66 percent in the same survey comparison.
claims.verbatim: groceries and food from 61% to 66%
claims.notes: Utilities rose 12 points against groceries 5, which is what makes the energy result distinctive rather than general gloom.

claims.claim: Worry about affording healthcare services rose from 57 percent to 66 percent and housing from 43 percent to 53 percent.
claims.value: 57 to 66 percent healthcare, 43 to 53 percent housing
claims.verbatim: healthcare services from 57% to 66%, and housing from 43% to 53%
claims.notes: Two figures from one clause serving one comparison.

claims.claim: Asked where an extra 100 million dollars of state spending should go, 39 percent of Alaska voters named making electricity and heating more affordable as a first or second choice, against 35 percent for the Permanent Fund Dividend and 33 percent for K-12 education.
claims.verbatim: energy affordability tops the list: 39% name it as their first or second choice, ahead of the PFD (35%) and K-12 education (33%)
claims.notes: MUST be printed as combined first AND second choice. On first choice alone the ranking inverts, see C14.

claims.claim: On first choice alone, Alaska voters most commonly named the Permanent Fund Dividend at 26 percent, then K-12 public education at 22 percent, with making electricity and heating more affordable third at 17 percent.
claims.verbatim: voters most commonly cite the Permanent Fund Dividend (PFD) as their first choice at 26%, followed by K-12 public education (22%) and making electricity and heating more affordable (17%)
claims.notes: The counterweight to C13 from the same post. Energy leads on combined first plus second and trails on first alone, which is a real finding about breadth versus intensity. 17 rising to 39, 26 to 35, 22 to 33.

claims.claim: Energy affordability topped the combined first and second choice list in the Fairbanks North Star Borough at 55 percent.
claims.verbatim: It tops the combined first and second choice list in the Kenai Peninsula (51%), Mat-Su (46%), and Fairbanks North Star (55%).
claims.notes: Borough subgroup of a 605 person sample. Do not compare boroughs to each other as if the gaps were significant.

claims.claim: Energy affordability topped the combined first and second choice list on the Kenai Peninsula at 51 percent.
claims.verbatim: It tops the combined first and second choice list in the Kenai Peninsula (51%), Mat-Su (46%), and Fairbanks North Star (55%).
claims.notes: Same small subgroup caveat as C15.

claims.claim: Energy affordability topped the combined first and second choice list in the Mat-Su at 46 percent.
claims.verbatim: It tops the combined first and second choice list in the Kenai Peninsula (51%), Mat-Su (46%), and Fairbanks North Star (55%).
claims.notes: The Mat-Su is where the Houston vote sits, so this is the one borough figure that earns its place beside the Houston beat.

claims.claim: 60 percent of Alaska voters say their local electric utility should build a project that could raise bills for a few years but lower them over the following two decades, while 25 percent say it should not.
claims.verbatim: 60% say their local electric utility should build a project that could raise bills for a few years but lower them over the following two decades, while 25% say it should not
claims.notes: Sums to 85 with 15 unsure or no answer, a normal residual and a good sign the figures were not rebased.

claims.claim: 52 percent of Alaska voters say a utility that rejects such a project should be required to open its finances to an independent audit.
claims.verbatim: a majority of voters (52%) say it should be required to open its finances to an independent audit
claims.notes: Print the audit finding without an 'if rates rise' conditional, which no captured verbatim carries.

claims.claim: An ordinance to block data center construction within Houston city limits failed on a 4 to 2 vote.
claims.verbatim: An ordinance to block data center construction within Houston city limits failed 4-2, with council members Callie Courtney and Lisa Johansen voting yes.
claims.notes: Reported by Amy Bushatz. SINGLE SOURCED. Alaska Public Media and ADN carry the identical text as republication with permission, so they are syndication and not independent corroboration. Attribute to the Mat-Su Sentinel.

claims.claim: The Houston city council vote on the data center ordinance took place on August 13th, 2026.
claims.notes: WEAKEST SURVIVING CLAIM. Two reads returned August 13, 2026 but no verbatim sentence carrying the date was captured. If a slide prints the date it says 'as reported by the Mat-Su Sentinel'.

claims.claim: Houston council members Callie Courtney and Lisa Johansen voted in favor of the data center ban ordinance.
claims.verbatim: with council members Callie Courtney and Lisa Johansen voting yes
claims.notes: The article names only the two yes votes and not the four no votes. Do not characterise motives beyond the vote.

claims.claim: The Houston city council unanimously approved two resolutions opposing the state Department of Natural Resources land transfer process on the same night the ban failed.
claims.verbatim: The council unanimously approved two resolutions opposing DNR's land transfer process
claims.notes: The sharpest nuance available. One resolution concerned the AIDEA property and one an unrelated parcel bound for the state housing finance corporation.

claims.claim: Houston council member Jeffrey Brasel said of the state land transfer process that there was zero transparency and that preliminary decisions were made before the city had a decision to make.
claims.verbatim: There was zero transparency. They had made preliminary decisions before we made or even had a decision to make.
claims.notes: Verified verbatim on a second targeted fetch. An earlier paraphrase labelled 'adapted from original' must not be used.

claims.claim: Houston Mayor Carter Cole said that if a good reason were found for a data center in Houston it could probably end up in Houston and that without action now the city may never get that chance again.
claims.value: may never get that chance again
claims.verbatim: If we came up with a good reason why it should be in Houston, it could probably end up in Houston. If we don't take that action now, we may never get that chance again.
claims.notes: The counterweight voice. Including it protects the deck from framing the Houston vote as pure capitulation.

claims.claim: Houston official Kent Mitchell said that zoning laws preventing anyone from coming in and doing whatever they want would solve a future problem for multiple industries.
claims.verbatim: If our zoning laws are such that nobody can come in and just do whatever they want, then that solves a problem in the future for multiple industries
claims.notes: Describe Mitchell only as quoted in the Mat-Su Sentinel report, not by a title. This is the zoning versus ban argument in one line, which is the real substance of why the ban lost.

claims.claim: State Representative Kevin McCabe said what he supports is finding ways to get the city of Houston more revenue and the state more revenue.
claims.verbatim: What I do support is finding ways to get the city of Houston more revenue, the state more revenue.
claims.notes: The quote continues that if the city decides the land is more useful for trails, dog mushing and hiking, that is fully up to them and he supports it.

claims.claim: A Department of Natural Resources spokesperson said the city's resolutions will be reviewed as part of the proposal process if they are officially submitted as comments.
claims.verbatim: The city's resolutions will be reviewed as part of the proposal process if they're officially submitted as comments
claims.notes: Attributed in the article to DNR spokesperson Lorraine Henry. Gives the state's side, which the deck needs if it prints the zero transparency quote.

claims.claim: The proposed transfer would move 30 square miles of rural land from the Alaska Department of Natural Resources to the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority.
claims.verbatim: The proposed transfer would move 30 square miles of rural land from the Alaska Department of Natural Resources to the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority, or AIDEA.
claims.notes: Scale anchor only. This deck does not retell the conveyance, which No.14 already covered.

claims.claim: The proposed parcels border Willow, Meadow Lakes and Houston, with a small section crossing into Houston city limits.
claims.value: a small section inside city limits
claims.verbatim: The proposed parcels, currently held by DNR, border Willow, Meadow Lakes and Houston, with a small section crossing into Houston city limits
claims.notes: Important limiting fact. Houston's ban would only ever have reached a small section of the land in question, which the deck says if it calls the vote decisive.

claims.claim: Public Citizen's tracker of election deepfake legislation lists no enacted Alaska law, showing every Alaska bill as failed or with its election deepfake provision removed.
claims.verbatim: Introduced Jan. 2025, Passed Senate May 2025, Passed House 2026, Election deepfake provision removed
claims.notes: Independent tracker, replacing the ADN opinion column the scouts relied on. Verbatim shown is the SB 64 status row. Tracker also lists Alaska SB 2 and SB 33 as failed May 2026 and HB 358, SB 177 and HB 306 as failed in 2024.

claims.claim: Alaska Senate Bill 64 passed the House in 2026 with its election deepfake provision removed.
claims.verbatim: Introduced Jan. 2025, Passed Senate May 2025, Passed House 2026, Election deepfake provision removed
claims.notes: Shows the Legislature actively stripping AI language rather than merely failing to act. Attribute to Public Citizen's tracker. The akleg BASIS page it links returns 403 to automated requests, so the removal is not confirmed against the bill text.

claims.claim: At least 27 states are listed as having enacted election deepfake laws on Public Citizen's tracker as of its August 3rd, 2026 update.
claims.notes: DOWNGRADED from the scouts' 'roughly 30 states'. The tracker publishes no summary count, so this is a tally of its table. Print as 'at least 27 states, by a count of Public Citizen's tracker' or use only the Alaska half. Never 'about 30'.

claims.claim: The Anchorage Assembly adopted Ordinance AO 2026-27 on March 27th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: On March 27, 2026, the Anchorage Assembly adopted Ordinance AO 2026-27
claims.notes: Law firm client alert, a secondary write up. The muni.org primary PDF would not decode and the Assembly meetings index returned 404.

claims.claim: Ordinance AO 2026-27 amends Title 21 of the Anchorage Municipal Code by creating a new land use category for data centers.
claims.verbatim: amends Title 21 of the Anchorage Municipal Code by creating a new land use category for "data centers"
claims.notes: Same secondary sourcing caveat as C34.

claims.claim: Under the Anchorage ordinance data centers must obtain a conditional use permit, which triggers a discretionary review process.
claims.verbatim: must obtain a conditional use permit, triggering a discretionary review process
claims.notes: The crux of the deck's argument. Anchorage regulates how a data center gets approved. It does not stop one.

claims.claim: The Anchorage ordinance requires applicants to demonstrate that sufficient electrical, water and wastewater capacity exists to support the proposed facility.
claims.verbatim: Applicants must demonstrate that sufficient electrical, water, and wastewater capacity exists to support the proposed facility.
claims.notes: CORRECTED. The burden is on the APPLICANT to demonstrate capacity, not on a utility to file a statement.

claims.claim: The Anchorage ordinance is described as a land use and permitting framework for data centers and not as a moratorium.
claims.verbatim: a new land use and permitting framework for data centers
claims.notes: Confirms Anchorage is not a pause. The source also characterises the ordinance as an effort to proactively legislate.

claims.claim: In early and preliminary counting from Alaska's August 18th, 2026 primary, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins led the governor's race with 21.8 percent and Tom Begich followed with 19.7 percent.
claims.verbatim: Some 70% of precincts have reported results so far.
claims.notes: PRELIMINARY and the claim says so. Alaska Public Media and ADN independently report the same four percentages, which is real corroboration. The verbatim proves the state of the count rather than the percentages.

claims.claim: In the same preliminary count Bernadette Wilson had 10.7 percent and Dave Bronson 8.5 percent.
claims.verbatim: Votes are still being counted, and the results could change significantly in subsequent updates.
claims.notes: Corroborated by ADN at the same figures. The verbatim again carries the caveat rather than the figures.

claims.claim: The Alaska governor primary field included 17 candidates made up of 12 Republicans, three independents and two Democrats.
claims.verbatim: 17 candidates, including 12 Republicans, three independents and two Democrats
claims.notes: 12 plus 3 plus 2 equals 17. ADN only.

claims.claim: Under Alaska's election laws the top four vote getters in the primary advance to the general election regardless of party.
claims.verbatim: Under Alaska's election laws, the top four vote-getters, regardless of party affiliation, will advance to the general election.
claims.notes: Say top four advance to a general election in November. Do not assert ranked choice or an exact November date.

claims.claim: Alaska election officials plan to certify the primary results on August 31st, 2026.
claims.verbatim: Election officials are set to certify the results on Aug. 31.
claims.notes: Corroborated by Alaska Public Media. ADN also reports further counting on August 25th and 28th, and that ballots may arrive until August 28th.

claims.claim: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wrote that he is the first and he believes still the only candidate in the governor's race to call for a moratorium on data center development in Alaska until the state can pass comprehensive regulation.
claims.verbatim: candidate in the governor's race to call for a moratorium on data center development in Alaska until the state can pass comprehensive regulation that protects the public interest.
claims.notes: Primary as a statement of the author's own position, published under his own byline six days before he led the primary count. The first and only self description is his claim and the claim text attributes it to him.

claims.claim: Over two dozen demonstrators affiliated with the group PauseAI took to the streets of Anchorage on a Monday afternoon warning drivers about the under regulation of AI.
claims.verbatim: On Monday afternoon, over two dozen demonstrators affiliated with the group PauseAI took to the streets of Anchorage
claims.notes: DISCREPANCY RESOLVED. ONE event, not two. Published August 13th, 2026, a Thursday, saying 'On Monday afternoon', which is August 10th. Alaska's News Source's later piece refers to 'last Monday's protest', the same day. No fetched page prints the date as a numeral, so say 'a Monday in mid August' or attribute the date.

killed.claim: House Bill 47 criminalising AI generated child sexual abuse material and deepfake harassment became law in June 2026
killed.why: No source reachable. akleg BASIS 403, LegiScan 403, trackbill did not resolve, the governor's newsroom index showed no such release, and four search engines returned CAPTCHA or 403. Zero pages fetched that mention this bill.

killed.claim: House Bill 47 is Alaska's only substantive AI statute
killed.why: Depends on the killed HB 47 claim, and is additionally an unbounded negative about the whole Alaska statute book that no fetched page supports.

killed.claim: House Concurrent Resolution 3 would have created a Joint Legislative Task Force on Artificial Intelligence and stalled without producing a report
killed.why: No primary or secondary record reached. BASIS 403s, and the Kreiss-Tomkins op-ed contains no mention of HCR 3, so even an attributed assertion has no named source behind it.

killed.claim: Roughly 30 states have election related deepfake disclosure laws
killed.why: Public Citizen's tracker publishes no total and a tally of its table gives at least 27 distinct states, not about 30. Survives only in the hedged form at C33.

killed.claim: Anchorage adopted AO 2026-27 on a 10 to 2 vote
killed.why: The tally appears on no readable page. The adoption survives at C34, the tally does not.

killed.claim: The Anchorage ordinance requires utility statements on system capacity
killed.why: Misstates the source, which places the burden on the applicant to demonstrate capacity. Replaced by C37.

killed.claim: The Houston city council has six members
killed.why: Council size is not published in the original or the republication. Inferring a body's size from one roll call is not verification.

killed.claim: No moratorium or pause on data centers exists anywhere in Alaska at state, borough or city level as of today
killed.why: An unbounded negative that was not established. Two jurisdictions were checked out of one state, nineteen organised boroughs, the unorganised borough and every incorporated city. The deck MAY say 'no pause has been adopted in the places that have voted on one' or 'Alaska has adopted no statewide pause'. It may NOT say 'nowhere in Alaska'.

killed.claim: The Alaska general election is on November 3rd, 2026
killed.why: Neither fetched article prints a date. Both say only November.

killed.claim: About 283 of 402 precincts had reported in the primary
killed.why: No raw precinct counts on either page. Both report 70 percent of precincts reporting. The 283 of 402 figure is a back calculation.

killed.claim: The top four primary finishers advance to a ranked choice general election
killed.why: Top four advancing is verified at C42, but neither article describes the general as ranked choice.

killed.claim: 122,477 ballots had been counted in the primary
killed.why: Never captured inside a verbatim string and Alaska Public Media does not carry it. Dropped in favour of the 70 percent of precincts figure both outlets state.

killed.claim: A PauseAI demonstration took place in Anchorage on August 17th, 2026
killed.why: That was a publication date, not an event date. Two scouts reported one event as two.

killed.claim: The exact wording of the Data for Progress data center question
killed.why: Not published in the announcement post, and the linked toplines PDF would not decode, so no wording was ever seen. C09 records this gap explicitly.

killed.claim: 52 percent support requiring an audit if rates rise
killed.why: The 52 percent audit figure survives at C19, but the 'if rates rise' condition appears in no captured verbatim.

killed.claim: Alaska Public Media independently corroborates the Houston vote
killed.why: It does not. It republished the Mat-Su Sentinel with permission, as did ADN. The Houston beat is single sourced to reporter Amy Bushatz and the deck must attribute it.
